summary: Specifies what network devices must do to provide Controlled-Load service, which gives a flow behavior close to that of a lightly loaded network even when real traffic is heavy. It is part of the integrated services work.

plainLanguage.summary: Controlled-Load is a service a router can offer to one particular flow. The router first checks that it has room for the traffic the flow promises, and then treats that flow almost as if the network were empty. The aim is to keep a call or a video stream working while other traffic fills the link.

subtitle: What a router must do to give a flow the experience of a lightly loaded network, even when the network is busy.

tldr.problem: Real-time applications such as audio and video work well on a quiet network but fall apart quickly when the network is busy, and best-effort service gives them no protection.
tldr.mechanism: A flow describes the traffic it will send with a TSpec, a token bucket plus a peak rate and packet size limits. Each network element uses admission control to accept only the flows it can carry, then serves accepted flows so that they behave as they would on an unloaded network.
tldr.outcome: The service is intentionally minimal: one function, no optional capabilities, and no numeric delay or loss targets. Traffic that exceeds the flow's TSpec is not dropped outright but forwarded best-effort if resources allow.

facts.label: Bucket rate range
facts.value: 1 byte per second to 40 terabytes per second

facts.label: Conformance bound
facts.value: Data sent must not exceed rT+b over any period T

facts.label: Burst time
facts.value: Time to transmit the maximum size data burst at the requested rate

today: RFC 2211 is a Proposed Standard published in September 1997. The metadata for this unit records no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is part of the integrated services work and was written to be used with RSVP, described in RFC 2205.

sections.title: What the Service Is
sections.content:
RFC 2211 defines the behavior required of network elements that support the Controlled-Load service. It is one of a series of documents that specify the network element behavior required to support various qualities of service in IP internetworks, and the services they describe are useful both in the global Internet and in private IP networks. The document is based on the service specification template given in RFC 2216.

Section 3 gives the motivation. The service is intended to support a broad class of applications developed for use in today's Internet that are highly sensitive to overloaded conditions, in particular the adaptive real-time applications that work well on unloaded networks but degrade quickly under overload. A service that mimics an unloaded network serves those applications well. The service is intentionally minimal, with no optional functions or capabilities in the specification: it offers only a single function, so system and application designers can assume that all implementations are identical in that respect.

Internally, the service suits a wide range of implementation techniques, including evolving scheduling and admission control algorithms that let an implementation use network resources efficiently. It is equally amenable to extremely simple implementation where maximum utilization of network resources is not the only concern.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the specification for one of the guaranteed-quality services in IP networks. It is aimed at applications such as live audio and video, which work well on a quiet network and fall apart on a busy one.

sections.title: What an Application May Assume
sections.content:
The end-to-end behavior provided to an application by a series of network elements providing controlled-load service tightly approximates the behavior visible to applications receiving best-effort service under unloaded conditions. Assuming the network is functioning correctly, these applications may assume that a very high percentage of transmitted packets will be successfully delivered by the network to the receiving end-nodes, with the percentage of packets not successfully delivered closely approximating the basic packet error rate of the transmission medium. They may also assume that the transit delay experienced by a very high percentage of the delivered packets will not greatly exceed the minimum transmit delay experienced by any successfully delivered packet, a figure that includes speed-of-light delay plus the fixed processing time in routers and other communications devices along the path.

To make sure those conditions are met, a client requesting controlled-load service gives the intermediate network elements an estimate of the data traffic it will generate, the TSpec. In return, the service ensures that network element resources adequate to process traffic falling within that descriptive envelope will be available to the client. If the client's traffic generation properties fall outside the region described by the TSpec parameters, the quality of service may exhibit characteristics indicative of overload, including large numbers of delayed or dropped packets. The service definition does not require that this overload behaviour match what a best-effort data flow would receive on the same path.

The RFC notes that the term "unloaded" is used in the sense of not heavily loaded or congested, rather than in the sense of no other network traffic whatsoever.
sections.plainLanguage: An application can expect its packets to arrive almost as quickly and as reliably as they would on an empty network. The price is that the client must first describe the traffic it intends to send.

sections.title: What the Network Element Must Do
sections.content:
Each network element accepting a request for controlled-load service must ensure that adequate bandwidth and packet processing resources are available to handle the requested level of traffic, as given by the requestor's TSpec. This must be accomplished through active admission control, and all resources important to the operation of the element must be considered. Common examples are link bandwidth, router or switch port buffer space, and the computational capacity of the packet forwarding engine.

The service does not accept or make use of specific target values for control parameters such as delay or loss. Instead, acceptance of a request implies a commitment by the network element to provide service closely equivalent to that provided to uncontrolled best-effort traffic under lightly loaded conditions. The RFC defines this quality of service by describing the events expected not to occur with any frequency: little or no average packet queueing delay, and little or no congestion loss, over all timescales significantly larger than the burst time. The burst time is the time required for the flow's maximum size data burst to be transmitted at the flow's requested transmission rate. Occasional congestion losses may occur, but any substantial sustained loss represents a failure of the admission control algorithm.

Two obligations follow. The implementation has to make bandwidth greater than the TSpec token rate available to the flow in certain situations, because if a flow received exactly its promised rate at all times, queueing caused by an over-rate burst might never clear and the traffic queueing delay would permanently increase. At minimum, a mechanism must be present to borrow the bandwidth needed to clear bursts, ranging from explicit borrowing schemes within the traffic scheduler to implicit schemes based on statistical multiplexing and measurement-based admission control. Buffer management must likewise have flexibility, because the service does not reshape traffic to its token-bucket parameters at every node, so traffic is distorted as it traverses queueing points, particularly during bursts; an implementation should be prepared to make additional buffering available to bursting flows, for example by statistical multiplexing of a shared buffer pool.

Links are not permitted to fragment packets that receive controlled-load service, and packets larger than the MTU of the link are treated as nonconformant to the TSpec. The service requires no control of short-term packet delay jitter beyond the description above, though the use of scheduling algorithms that add jitter control is not prohibited. Packet losses from non-congestion causes, such as link errors, are not bounded by this service.
sections.plainLanguage: Before accepting a flow, a router checks that it has the bandwidth and buffer space to carry it. After accepting, it must make sure the flow is not slowed down or dropped for long periods, and it must be able to lend the flow a little extra bandwidth to absorb a sudden burst.

sections.title: Invocation Information and the TSpec
sections.content:
The service is invoked by specifying the desired traffic parameters of the data flow to the network element. A request for a new flow is accepted if the element has the capacity to forward the flow's packets as described. A request to change the TSpec of an existing flow is treated as a new invocation, so admission control is reapplied, while a request that reduces the TSpec, in the sense that the new TSpec is strictly smaller under the ordering rules, should never be denied service.

The service uses the TOKEN_BUCKET_TSPEC defined in RFC 2215: a token bucket specification plus a peak rate p, a minimum policed unit m and a maximum packet size M. The token bucket has a rate r and a depth b, and both must be positive. The rate is measured in bytes of IP datagrams per second and may range from 1 byte per second to 40 terabytes per second, while the depth is measured in bytes and may range from 1 byte to 250 gigabytes. The element MUST return an error for values outside those ranges, and also for any value inside the range that the element cannot support. The ranges are large on purpose, to allow for future network technologies, and no element is expected to support the full range.

The peak rate p is measured like the bucket rate and has the same range. It exists in this version mainly for TSpec compatibility with other QoS control services, and the field may always be ignored by a conforming service. The minimum policed unit m is an integer measured in bytes, and all IP datagrams smaller than m count against the token bucket as being of size m. The maximum packet size M is the biggest packet that conforms to the traffic specification. Both m and M must be positive, m must be less than or equal to M, and a service request must be rejected if the requested maximum packet size is larger than the MTU of the link.

The preferred concrete representation is three floating point numbers in single-precision IEEE format followed by two 32-bit integers in network byte order: the rate r, the bucket size b, the peak rate p, the minimum policed unit m and the maximum packet size M. Negative numbers, infinities and NANs are not allowed for r and b, and the RFC asks implementations to verify arriving parameters against these rules before using them in floating point computations. The controlled-load service is assigned service_name 5, and the TOKEN_BUCKET_TSPEC parameter used by it is general parameter number 127.
sections.plainLanguage: The client describes its traffic with five numbers: the average rate it will send, the size of the bucket that allows short bursts, a peak rate, the smallest packet that will be counted, and the largest packet it will send. A router that cannot meet those numbers rejects the request.

sections.title: Policing and Traffic That Breaks the Rules
sections.content:
The service is provided to a flow on the basis that the flow's traffic conforms to the TSpec given at setup time. The token bucket parameters require that over all time periods the amount of data sent does not exceed rT+b, where r and b are the token bucket parameters and T is the length of the period. For that accounting, links must count packets smaller than the minimal policing unit m as being of size m. Packets that arrive at an element and break the rT+b bound are considered nonconformant, and so are packets bigger than the outgoing link MTU.

In the presence of nonconformant packets, each network element must ensure locally that three requirements are met: it MUST continue to provide the contracted quality of service to the controlled-load flows not experiencing excess traffic; it SHOULD prevent excess controlled-load traffic from unfairly impacting the handling of arriving best-effort traffic; and, consistent with those two, it MUST attempt to forward the excess traffic on a best-effort basis if sufficient resources are available.

Network elements must not assume that the arrival of nonconformant traffic for a controlled-load flow will be unusual or indicative of error. In certain circumstances, particularly routers acting as the split points of a multicast distribution tree supporting a shared reservation, large numbers of packets fail the conformance test as a matter of normal operation. Elements must also not assume that data sources or upstream elements have already policed controlled-load flows, so each element providing the service MUST independently meet the requirements above. Examples of suitable mechanisms include token-bucket policing filters and per-flow scheduling algorithms; placing all controlled-load flows into the same shared resource pool without first ensuring that nonconformant flows cannot starve conformant ones is insufficient.

Beyond those requirements, the service does not define the quality of service delivered to flows with nonconformant arriving traffic. It is permissible either to degrade the service delivered to all of the flow's packets equally, or to sort the flow's packets into a conformant set and a nonconformant set and deliver different levels of service to the two.
sections.plainLanguage: If a flow sends more than it promised, the router does not simply throw the extra packets away. It keeps serving the promised rate, and forwards the excess in the background if there is room.

sections.title: Ordering and Merging TSpecs
sections.content:
One TSpec is a substitute for another, meaning as good or better than, if and only if its token bucket rate r is greater than or equal to that of the other, its bucket depth b is greater than or equal, its peak rate p is greater than or equal, its minimum policed unit m is less than or equal, and its maximum packet size M is greater than or equal. Not all TSpecs can be ordered with respect to each other: if two differ but not all five conditions hold, they are unordered.

A merged TSpec is the TSpec used by the RSVP protocol when merging a set of TSpecs to create a merged reservation. The merged parameters are used as the traffic flow's TSpec at the local node, and they are passed upstream to the traffic sources to describe the characteristics of the reservation actually installed along the data path. For controlled-load service, the merged TSpec is calculated over a set of TSpecs by taking the largest token bucket rate, the largest token bucket size, the largest peak rate, the smallest minimum policed unit and the smallest maximum packet size.

A Least Common TSpec is a TSpec adequate to describe the traffic from any one of a number of flows. It can be useful when creating a shared reservation using SNMP or another management protocol. It differs from the merged TSpec in that its computed parameters are not passed upstream to the sources of traffic. It takes the largest token bucket rate, the largest token bucket size, the largest peak rate, the smallest minimum policed unit and the largest maximum packet size.

The sum of n controlled-load service TSpecs is used when computing the TSpec for a shared reservation of n flows. It adds the token bucket rate, the token bucket size and the peak rate across all TSpecs, and takes the minimum of the minimum policed units and the maximum of the maximum packet sizes. The minimum of two TSpecs differs according to whether they can be ordered: for unordered TSpecs it takes the smaller token bucket rate, the larger token bucket size, the smaller peak rate, the smaller minimum policed unit and the smaller maximum packet size.
sections.plainLanguage: When several flows share one reservation, their descriptions have to be combined into one. The rules say which numbers to take from which flow, so that every router in the path makes the same choice.

sections.title: Guidelines for Implementors
sections.content:
On admission control, the intention of the service is that network elements deliver a level of service closely approximating best-effort service under unloaded conditions, and it is not required that every single packet be delivered with zero queueing delay. Elements are permitted to oversubscribe resources to some extent, in the sense that the bandwidth and buffer requirements indicated by summing the TSpec token buckets of all controlled-load flows may exceed the maximum capabilities of the element. This may only be done where the element is quite sure that actual utilization is less than that sum suggests, based on measurement of aggregate traffic, knowledge of application traffic statistics or other means. The most conservative approach, rejecting new flows whenever their addition would push the strict sum of the token buckets past the element's capacity, may be appropriate in other circumstances.

On interaction with best-effort traffic, the RFC warns that if the element's best-effort queueing algorithm does not distinguish between excess controlled-load packets and elastic best-effort traffic such as TCP flows, the excess controlled-load packets will back off the elastic traffic and dominate the best-effort bandwidth usage. Two basic approaches are available: the element can maintain separate resource allocations for different classes of best-effort traffic, or it can process excess controlled-load traffic at a somewhat lower priority than elastic best-effort traffic. If most controlled-load traffic comes from non-rate-adaptive real-time applications, priority mechanisms might be desirable; if it comes from rate-adaptive or elastic applications, separate resource classes might be preferable. The choice depends on the design goals and the implementation techniques available, and the specification leaves it to the implementor.

On forwarding behavior with nonconformant traffic, degrading the service to all of the flow's packets equally keeps reordering at low levels, which suits applications and transport protocols sensitive to excessive reordering, such as an unmodified TCP connection that would see reordering as lost packets and trigger duplicate acknowledgements. Sorting the packets into a conformant and a nonconformant set delivers some packets with low loss and delay and others with higher loss and potentially higher delay, which may be preferable for highly time-sensitive applications such as interactive conferencing tools.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC tells implementers how to judge the service: compare the delay and loss of a controlled flow with the same flow on an empty network, then add load and see whether those numbers stay put. It also warns that a router must not let excess controlled-load traffic squeeze out ordinary traffic such as TCP.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A network element implementing the service described here is intentionally and explicitly expected to give preferential treatment to selected packet traffic. This memo does not describe the mechanism used to indicate which traffic is to receive that preferential treatment, because the controlled-load service may be invoked by a number of mechanisms, including RSVP, SNMP network management software, or proprietary control software. However, any mechanism used to invoke the service must provide security sufficient to guard against the use of this preferential treatment capability by undesired or unauthorized traffic.

A correct implementation of the service is not susceptible to a denial-of-service attack based on maliciously requesting a very small resource allocation for the attacked traffic flow, because the specification requires that traffic in excess of the requested level be carried on a best-effort basis rather than being dropped.

Of necessity, giving preferential service to certain traffic flows implies giving less service to other flows. It is therefore possible to conduct a denial of service attack by maliciously reconfiguring the admission control algorithm to allow overallocation of available bandwidth or other forwarding resources, starving non-controlled-load flows. In general the RFC judges this unlikely to increase the network's vulnerability to attack, because many other reconfigurations of a router or host can cause denial of service in the same way, and it is reasonable to assume that whatever protects against other reconfiguration attacks will protect against this one too.
sections.plainLanguage: Preferring some traffic over others is the whole point of the service, so the way the preference is requested has to be protected. Otherwise an attacker could ask for the whole link and starve everyone else.

viz.caption: WHAT A CONTROLLED-LOAD FLOW MAY EXPECT

items.title: Delivery
items.text: A very high percentage of transmitted packets reaches the far end.

items.title: Delay
items.text: The delay of delivered packets stays close to the minimum any packet sees.

items.title: Loss
items.text: Lost packets stay close to the error rate of the transmission medium.

items.title: Outside the TSpec
items.text: Traffic beyond the declared envelope may be delayed or dropped.

cells: Quality falls as the network fills
Accepted flows behave as they would on an unloaded network
Resources are reserved for the flow through admission control
None; the promise is unloaded-like behaviour
Forwarded on a best-effort basis if resources allow

items.label: Bucket rate
items.desc: Bytes of IP datagrams per second; 1 byte per second to 40 terabytes per second.

items.label: Peak rate
items.desc: Bytes per second, same range as r. A conforming service may always ignore it.

items.label: Minimum policed unit
items.desc: Smaller datagrams count against the bucket as if they were this size.

items.label: Maximum packet size
items.desc: Biggest conforming packet. A request above the link MTU must be rejected.
